lessons.name: CoppeliaSim
lessons.summary: CoppeliaSim is a robotics simulator where scripts control virtual robots, sensors and physical interactions before you try them on hardware.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
CoppeliaSim is a robotics simulator where scripts control virtual robots, sensors and physical interactions before you try them on hardware.

![CoppeliaSim BubbleRob robot with two wheels, a sensing nose and surrounding obstacles.](/img/lessons/robots_simulator_tool_2-coppeliasim.webp)
*BubbleRob, the wheeled robot built in the official tutorial. Source: [Publisher](https://manual.coppeliarobotics.com/en/bubbleRobTutorial.htm), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **A visible debugging playground**: watch a robot react to your code without first wiring motors or buying an arm.
- **Software analogy**: a scene is an integration-test environment; simulated sensors provide inputs, and motor commands produce observable changes.

## What it is made of / how it works
- **Scene objects** include shapes, joints and sensors. The scene hierarchy groups them into a robot model, rather like a tree of objects in a program.
- **Control code** can run inside the scene or connect from another program through a remote API, an interface for controlling the simulator externally.

| Property | Published detail |
|---|---|
| Embedded scripting | Python and Lua |
| BubbleRob drive | Two driven wheels |
| Tutorial proximity sensor | Detects obstacles ahead |
| Tutorial vision resolution | 256 × 256 pixels |
| Tutorial reverse interval | 4 seconds |

- **Worked example**: BubbleRob reads its proximity sensor. On detection, it reverses one wheel at half speed and the other at one-eighth speed, producing a curve.
- **Separate responsibilities**: the tutorial also records clearance on a graph and displays a vision-sensor image; neither replaces the obstacle-avoidance controller.

> **Key idea:** A simulator makes the connection between sensor readings and motor commands visible, not automatically correct.

## Key terms
- **Joint**: a movable connection; BubbleRob's wheel joints receive target angular speeds.
- **Proximity sensor**: a simulated detector reporting nearby objects, rather than a camera image.
- **Remote API**: commands sent by an external program instead of an embedded script.

## Getting started
1. **Check access:** choose a CoppeliaSim edition on the official site; check its licence for your use rather than assuming commercial use is free.
2. **Build BubbleRob:** follow the free tutorial through the wheels, sensing nose and obstacle cylinders.
3. **Run the example:** observe forward motion, obstacle detection, then curved reversing. Change the speed slider and compare the trace.
4. **Inspect the hierarchy:** identify which objects sense, move and display results before trying an external Python controller.

## Used in
- **Map connection**: Coppelia Robotics develops CoppeliaSim; use its simulator to practise the sensor-to-action relationship before a hardware project.

lessons.name: CortexBench
lessons.summary: CortexBench tests how useful pretrained visual representations are across different embodied-AI tasks, from navigation to manipulation.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
CortexBench tests how useful pretrained visual representations are across different embodied-AI tasks, from navigation to manipulation.

![CortexBench overview showing robot hands, arms and navigation environments.](/img/lessons/robots_simulator_tool_2-cortexbench.webp)
*The benchmark spans different bodies and tasks, not just one robot. Source: [Publisher](https://eai-vc.github.io/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Reuse vision**: a robot-learning project need not learn every visual feature from scratch. CortexBench helps test whether an existing image encoder transfers well.
- **Software analogy**: treat encoders like interchangeable library implementations and CortexBench like the shared test suite, not a single flattering demo.

## What it is made of / how it works
- **Input**: camera observations become vectors through a visual encoder. A task-specific policy uses those vectors to choose actions.
- **Comparison**: evaluate representations across tasks with different bodies and goals. The project compares frozen features with features adapted during task learning.

| Property | Published detail |
|---|---|
| Benchmark size | 17 tasks |
| Task families | Locomotion, navigation, dexterous and mobile manipulation |
| Released visual models | VC-1 and VC-1-base |
| VC-1 training video | Over 4,000 hours of egocentric video |
| VC-1 training images | Over 5.6 million images |

- **Worked example**: the VC-1-base notebook turns one image into a 1 × 3 × 224 × 224 tensor, then a 1 × 768 feature vector.
- **Read the dimensions**: the tensor stores batch, colour channels, height and width; the output holds numerical features, not a motor command.
- **Controlled experiment**: compare a frozen encoder with an adapted encoder while keeping the task fixed; the project demonstrates both approaches for mobile picking.

> **Key idea:** A useful visual representation must help an agent act, not merely recognize objects in photographs.

## Key terms
- **Encoder**: a model that turns an image into numerical features.
- **Embodied AI**: intelligence evaluated through an agent interacting with an environment.
- **Frozen features**: encoder weights stay unchanged while a downstream policy learns.
- **Fine-tuning**: updating pretrained weights for the task instead of leaving them fixed.

## Getting started
1. **Start free:** read the public project page and watch the paired mobile-picking videos to understand the evaluation question.
2. **Run the tutorial:** follow the official repository notebook for loading a visual model and transforming an image.
3. **Choose one task:** install its documented environment dependencies before attempting the whole benchmark; these are not a single universal simulator.
4. **Record the setup:** note model, frozen/adapted setting and task, so your comparison explains what changed.

## Used in
- **Robot-camera feature atlas** begins with inspecting representations; **Frozen-encoder low-data race** compares what those features enable.
- **Pretrained visual representations for robots** explains the underlying idea; **Policy evaluation & real-world testing methodology** helps interpret results.

lessons.name: CQL reference implementation
lessons.summary: The CQL reference implementation trains reinforcement-learning policies from existing datasets while penalizing overly optimistic values for unsupported actions.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
The CQL reference implementation trains reinforcement-learning policies from existing datasets while penalizing overly optimistic values for unsupported actions.

![CQL project diagram separating data collection, learning from a stored buffer and policy deployment.](/img/lessons/robots_simulator_tool_2-cql.webp)
*The authors illustrate the offline-learning workflow used by CQL. Source: [Publisher](https://sites.google.com/view/cql-offline-rl), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Learn from logs**: offline reinforcement learning uses previously collected transitions rather than collecting new experience during training.
- **The trap**: a learned value function can assign attractive scores to actions poorly represented in those logs, and the policy can exploit that mistake.
- **Software analogy**: imagine an optimizer discovering undefined behaviour outside your test coverage; CQL changes the objective instead of trusting every predicted score.

## What it is made of / how it works
- **Training input**: recorded states, actions, rewards and following states provide the experience for learning a policy, a rule for choosing actions.
- **Conservative learning**: the additional objective pushes values down under a chosen action distribution and up under the dataset distribution.

| Property | Published detail |
|---|---|
| Method | Conservative Q-Learning |
| Learning setting | Offline reinforcement learning |
| Reference experiment families | Atari and D4RL |
| Action settings | Discrete and continuous |
| Added ingredient | Q-value regularizer |
| Atari 1% replay setting | 1000 entries per individual buffer |
| Atari 10% replay setting | 10000 entries per individual buffer |

- **Worked example**: the Atari instructions use 1000 entries per individual replay buffer for 1% data, versus 10000 for 10%. Record the setting before comparing runs.
- **Dataset versions**: the README warns that changed D4RL datasets affect results; matching an algorithm name alone is insufficient.
- **Interpretation**: the paper's lower-bound result concerns expected policy value under its assumptions, not a hardware-safety certificate for every action.

> **Key idea:** High predicted reward is weak evidence when the dataset barely covers the proposed action.

## Key terms
- **Q-value**: predicted future return for taking an action in a state.
- **Return**: accumulated reward, often discounting rewards further in the future.
- **Out-of-distribution action**: an action unlike those supported by the training data.
- **Regularizer**: an extra training term that discourages an unwanted solution.

## Getting started
1. **Read and watch free:** use the authors' explanation, then the offline-RL lecture segment covering conservative value learning.
2. **Pick D4RL or Atari:** follow that folder's instructions; do not mix their dependencies and launch commands.
3. **Match the dataset:** record the environment and dataset version alongside the configuration before comparing published scores.
4. **Inspect values and returns:** compare both, rather than treating a rising predicted Q-value as evidence of better behaviour.

## Used in
- **Offline value optimism microscope** explores the failure mode; **CQL and IQL dataset-quality ladder** compares learning from different logs.
- **Offline reinforcement learning** supplies the conceptual background before an **Offline-policy release stress test**.

lessons.name: Crocoddyl
lessons.summary: Crocoddyl is an optimal-control library that computes robot motion and feedback policies for a specified sequence of contacts.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
Crocoddyl is an optimal-control library that computes robot motion and feedback policies for a specified sequence of contacts.

![Animated Crocoddyl robot-control demonstration shown in the official repository.](/img/lessons/robots_simulator_tool_2-crocoddyl.webp)
*A frame from a Crocoddyl repository demonstration. Source: [Publisher](https://github.com/loco-3d/crocoddyl), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Motion from objectives**: instead of scripting every joint angle, describe the robot, desired behaviour and penalties, then let a solver improve a candidate motion.
- **Software analogy**: it resembles an optimizing compiler: the model and objective describe the problem, while a numerical solver searches for a better executable trajectory.

## What it is made of / how it works
- **Dynamics model**: Pinocchio computes how the robot moves under forces. Crocoddyl builds an optimal-control problem around these calculations.
- **Contact sequence**: specify when feet or hands contact the environment. The library optimizes motion within that structure rather than inventing all contact choices.

| Property | Published detail |
|---|---|
| Core implementation | C++ |
| User bindings | Python |
| Dynamics library | Pinocchio |
| Solver family | DDP and FDDP |
| Published outputs | State trajectories and feedback policies |
| Cart-pole notebook state size | 4 variables |
| Cart-pole notebook control size | 1 force input |

- **Worked example**: the cart-pole notebook uses 50 running nodes, each lasting 0.05 seconds: a 2.5-second planning window for the cart-mounted pendulum.
- **Solver result**: examine both the simulated motion and optimization trace. A solved numerical problem only reflects the model and objectives you actually supplied.

> **Key idea:** State the desired outcome and contact structure; optimization fills in the detailed motion.

## Key terms
- **Trajectory**: robot states and commands arranged over time, not just a geometric line.
- **Optimal control**: choosing commands to minimize a cost while respecting the motion model.
- **DDP**: differential dynamic programming, a method that improves trajectories using local approximations.
- **FDDP**: feasibility-driven DDP, a related solver for improving candidate trajectories.
- **Feedback policy**: a command rule that also reacts to departures from the planned state.

## Getting started
1. **Start free:** watch the authors' demonstration and read the repository installation options for your environment.
2. **Open the cart-pole notebook:** identify the state, controls, running cost and terminal cost before launching the solver.
3. **Run the supplied example:** view the swing-up and inspect how cost changes during optimization.
4. **Change one cost:** rerun and explain the motion difference; leave humanoid contacts for after this small problem.

## Used in
- **Crocoddyl jump for a simulated quadruped** and **Humanoid jump with Crocoddyl** extend the same optimization structure to legged machines.
- **Trajectory-optimized motions as RL references** connects planned movements with learning.

lessons.name: cuRobo
lessons.summary: cuRobo is a CUDA-accelerated library for robot motion generation, including kinematics, collision checking and trajectory optimization.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
cuRobo is a CUDA-accelerated library for robot motion generation, including kinematics, collision checking and trajectory optimization.

![cuRobo demonstration with a real Franka arm and a wooden obstacle moving across its workspace.](/img/lessons/robots_simulator_tool_2-curobo.webp)
*A frame from the official dynamic Franka demonstration. Source: [Publisher](https://curobo.org/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Plan arm movement**: a reachable destination is not enough; the robot also needs a path that avoids obstacles and respects its configured limits.
- **Software analogy**: GPU planning resembles a batch job exploring many candidate solutions in parallel, rather than waiting for one candidate after another.

## What it is made of / how it works
- **Inputs**: a robot model, collision geometry, starting joint state and target pose describe the planning request.
- **Computation**: inverse kinematics finds candidate joint configurations; geometric planning and trajectory optimization help connect them without collisions.

| Property | Published detail |
|---|---|
| Execution platform | CUDA-capable GPU |
| Main software stack | PyTorch, CUDA and Warp |
| Planning components | Kinematics, collision checks, trajectory optimization |
| Current repository generation | cuRoboV2 |
| Legacy v1 API tag | v0.7.8 |

- **Worked example**: after the repository's setup, its headless GPU check reports planning success and writes a trajectory plot:

```bash
python -m curobo.examples.getting_started.motion_planning --mode pose
```

- **Inspect the result**: verify the start state and goal frame, then check the returned success status and trajectory clearance before adapting the example.
- **Runtime discipline**: construct solvers, allocate collision storage and warm up before repeated requests. Reusing these objects avoids confusing setup work with steady-state planning time.
- **Version boundary**: the repository warns that V2 changes the public API; do not paste v1 tutorial imports into a V2 installation.

> **Key idea:** Fast planning is useful only when the robot model, collision world and returned motion are valid.

## Key terms
- **Pose**: position plus orientation, expressed relative to a coordinate frame.
- **Inverse kinematics**: finding joint positions that place a tool at a target pose.
- **Collision geometry**: simplified shapes used to check contact, distinct from decorative rendering meshes.
- **Warmup**: preparing reusable GPU execution before measuring repeated solves.

## Getting started
1. **Check hardware:** the code is public under Apache 2.0, but GPU compute is not automatically free.
2. **Choose a generation:** follow the current repository workflow; use the explicit v1 tag only when intentionally reproducing legacy examples.
3. **Run a provided robot:** inspect the model and collision shapes before substituting your own arm.
4. **Test failure handling:** try an unreachable target in simulation and reject unsuccessful results instead of sending them onward.

## Used in
- **Plan around a tabletop obstacle** introduces **Collision-free arm motion generation**.
- **Compare MoveIt and cuRobo paths** and **GPU-parallel motion planning** explore planning choices and parallel computation.

lessons.name: DIAL-MPC
lessons.summary: DIAL-MPC is a training-free controller that samples and refines future motions to generate torque-level commands for legged robots.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
DIAL-MPC is a training-free controller that samples and refines future motions to generate torque-level commands for legged robots.

![DIAL-MPC diagram showing trajectory-level and action-level annealing of candidate control sequences.](/img/lessons/robots_simulator_tool_2-dial-mpc.webp)
*The official project illustrates two levels of sampling refinement. Source: [Publisher](https://lecar-lab.github.io/dial-mpc/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **A different route to walking**: DIAL-MPC demonstrates locomotion without first training a reinforcement-learning policy for the task.
- **Software analogy**: imagine repeatedly running speculative simulations, scoring the outcomes, committing only the next command and replanning with updated information.

## What it is made of / how it works
- **Sampling-based control**: simulate candidate action sequences, evaluate their costs and refine the samples toward better outcomes.
- **Diffusion-style annealing**: progressively refine the sampling distribution. Here diffusion describes the optimization method, not an image generator or a pretrained walking policy.
- **Full-order model**: plan using the robot's detailed dynamics rather than reducing the whole body to a simple point mass.

| Go2 trot configuration | Published value |
|---|---|
| Candidate samples, Nsample | 2048 |
| Sample horizon, Hsample | 16 |
| Refinement passes, Ndiffuse | 2 |
| Initial refinement passes | 10 |
| Control interval, dt | 0.02 s |
| Command type | Torque |

- **Worked example**: the supplied Go2 trot configuration uses a 0.02-second control interval: 50 updates per simulated second. Its sample horizon is 16, not 16 seconds.
- **Receding horizon**: after executing the first part of the plan, the controller solves again using the new state instead of blindly completing an old sequence.

> **Key idea:** Repeated online optimization can produce locomotion without a separately trained policy, but still needs a robot model and computation.

## Key terms
- **MPC**: model predictive control; predict ahead, apply the next command, then replan.
- **Torque**: a turning effort applied at a joint, different from requesting a joint position.
- **Horizon**: the future window considered by the optimizer.
- **Annealing**: gradually concentrating a search from broad exploration toward selected solutions.

## Getting started
1. **Start with simulation:** the code is public; follow the repository's Ubuntu, Python and CUDA setup rather than treating it as a hardware-free web demo.
2. **Choose the Go2 trot example:** inspect the configuration and identify sample count, time interval and gait.
3. **Run the documented simulation:** compare the resulting gait with the official videos before adjusting one parameter.
4. **Record the trade-off:** compare motion quality and compute time when changing sampling settings on the same machine.

## Used in
- **Training-free quadruped gaits with DIAL-MPC** builds on this controller.
- **Sampling-based & GPU-parallel MPC** explains the search strategy behind the demonstrations.

lessons.name: DiffMJX
lessons.summary: DiffMJX improves gradient information in MuJoCo XLA contact simulations so optimization can better learn how actions change physical outcomes.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
DiffMJX improves gradient information in MuJoCo XLA contact simulations so optimization can better learn how actions change physical outcomes.

![DiffMJX paper figure illustrating simulation, muscles and a robot body.](/img/lessons/robots_simulator_tool_2-diffmjx.webp)
*A published figure from the DiffMJX research paper. Source: [Publisher](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.14186v1), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Learning through physics**: optimization needs to know how a small action change affects the result, especially when objects begin or stop touching.
- **Software analogy**: automatic differentiation is like tracing dependencies through a program; abrupt collision decisions can make that trace unhelpful even when the animation looks convincing.

## What it is made of / how it works
- **Adaptive integration**: vary numerical time steps to reduce errors that can contaminate gradients, rather than assuming one fixed step works everywhere.
- **Contact from a distance**: provide a gradient signal before contact. Straight-through estimation can keep these helper forces out of the forward simulation.
- **Separate questions**: the forward pass predicts motion; the backward pass estimates how changing inputs would change that motion.

| Property | Published detail |
|---|---|
| Simulator foundation | MuJoCo XLA, also called MJX |
| Array and differentiation framework | JAX |
| Adaptive integration library | Diffrax |
| Demonstrated toy problem | One-dimensional point mass |
| Repository requirement | Python 3.12+ |
| GPU acceleration requirement | CUDA 12 |

- **Worked example**: after setup and component access, run the supplied one-dimensional point-mass experiment. Compare how time-step settings affect derivatives, not only final positions.

```bash
uv run experiments/01_toyexample/run.py
```
- **Current access limitation**: the repository's setup lists SSH access to private component repositories. Public documentation does not imply every dependency is anonymously installable.

> **Key idea:** A plausible simulated trajectory and a useful gradient are different things; optimization needs both.

## Key terms
- **Gradient**: the sensitivity of an output or loss to a small input change.
- **Differentiable simulation**: simulation designed to support computing these sensitivities.
- **Contact**: physical interaction when bodies touch, often introducing abrupt changes.
- **Straight-through estimation**: using a chosen backward-pass derivative while retaining a different forward computation.

## Getting started
1. **Start free with the project videos:** look at the optimization tasks and identify where contact must happen.
2. **Read prerequisites:** check component access before spending time on installation; do not assume the setup script can fetch private repositories.
3. **Inspect the toy experiment:** trace initial state, simulation outcome and gradient, even if dependency access prevents execution.
4. **If runnable, compare settings:** reproduce the provided gradient comparison before attempting a complete robot-learning task.

## Used in
- **Contact gradient breakage gallery** illustrates unreliable derivatives; **Gradient-based push policy** uses gradients to improve actions.
- **Contact dynamics & differentiable simulation** gives the broader mechanics and learning context.

lessons.name: Direct visual LiDAR calibration toolbox
lessons.summary: The Direct visual LiDAR calibration toolbox estimates the position and orientation between a camera and a LiDAR without a calibration target.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
The Direct visual LiDAR calibration toolbox estimates the position and orientation between a camera and a LiDAR without a calibration target.

![Calibration toolbox figure showing supported camera and LiDAR types beside an aligned point-cloud result.](/img/lessons/robots_simulator_tool_2-lidar-calibration.webp)
*The official repository shows camera–LiDAR alignment results. Source: [Publisher](https://github.com/koide3/direct_visual_lidar_calibration), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Align two sensors**: a camera sees pixels; LiDAR measures spatial points. Combining them requires knowing how their coordinate frames relate.
- **Software analogy**: calibration is an adapter between incompatible coordinate APIs. Correct data from both sensors can still combine incorrectly if the adapter is wrong.

## What it is made of / how it works
- **Inputs**: camera imagery, a LiDAR point cloud and the camera projection model describe the observations and how spatial points map into pixels.
- **Registration**: the toolbox aligns observations through direct pixel-level comparison, rather than requiring a specially placed calibration board.
- **Outputs**: an extrinsic transformation describes sensor-to-sensor rotation and translation; the viewer lets you inspect the resulting overlay.

| Property | Published detail |
|---|---|
| Target requirement | Target-less |
| Calibration style | Single-shot, automatic |
| Method | Direct pixel-level registration |
| Supported inputs | Multiple LiDAR and camera projection models |
| Example datasets | Livox and Ouster |
| Repository licence | MIT |

- **Worked example**: the official Livox dataset contains five ROS 2 bags. Start with one and inspect its points, image and camera-info topics before preprocessing.
- **Data compatibility**: the documentation warns that converted ROS 1 example bags have a camera-info checksum issue requiring manually specified camera parameters.

> **Key idea:** Calibration estimates the relationship between sensors, not the position of every object they observe.

## Key terms
- **LiDAR**: a sensor measuring distances with light, producing spatial samples called a point cloud.
- **Extrinsics**: rotation and translation between coordinate frames.
- **Intrinsics**: camera parameters describing projection inside the camera, distinct from its mounting pose.
- **Registration**: finding a transformation that aligns observations of the same scene.

## Getting started
1. **Use the free examples:** follow the official installation guide and download a supplied dataset before recording your own.
2. **Inspect the bag:** verify its sensor topics and camera parameters using the example instructions.
3. **Follow preprocessing and calibration:** use the documented dataset workflow, keeping track of input directories and generated results.
4. **Inspect the overlay:** look for alignment across the scene, not merely one matching edge; use this to learn what the transformation changes.

## Used in
- **Extrinsic & multi-sensor calibration** explains the geometry.
- **Remountable camera-LiDAR calibration target and fixture** adds a physical mounting project; this toolbox itself does not require a target.

lessons.name: DLR David variable-stiffness joints
lessons.summary: DLR David uses mechanically adjustable joint stiffness to combine compliant interaction with powerful movements in a humanoid research platform.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
DLR David uses mechanically adjustable joint stiffness to combine compliant interaction with powerful movements in a humanoid research platform.

![Annotated DLR David mechanism diagram showing variable-stiffness actuator arrangements.](/img/lessons/robots_simulator_tool_2-dlr-david.webp)
*DLR identifies the different variable-stiffness mechanisms used in David. Source: [Publisher](https://www.dlr.de/en/rm/research/robotic-systems/humanoids/david/mechatronics-of-david), CC BY-NC-ND 3.0.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Mechanics affects control**: a motor command does not act on a perfectly rigid machine. Springs change how forces and impacts travel through the robot.
- **Software analogy**: stiffness resembles a configurable response gain, but here part of the response comes from real mechanical springs, not only software.

## What it is made of / how it works
- **Variable-stiffness actuators**: motors and elastic mechanisms let the robot adjust how strongly a joint resists displacement.
- **Different mechanisms**: DLR describes antagonistic actuation, bidirectional antagonistic variable stiffness and floating spring joints across its hand-arm system.
- **Visible hardware**: the research platform exposes dense arrangements of motors, tendons and springs rather than hiding all actuation behind a smooth shell.

| David platform property | DLR's published value |
|---|---|
| Approximate mass | 55 kg |
| Degrees of freedom | 44 |
| Brushless DC motors | 83 |
| Position sensors | 173 |
| Joint stiffness | Variable in all joints |

- **Worked example**: 83 motors serve 44 degrees of freedom. This is not one motor per movable coordinate; the elastic, antagonistic architecture needs a richer actuator model.
- **Observation task**: watch David drill and hammer into concrete, then identify where mechanical compliance matters when forces change abruptly.

> **Key idea:** Some robot behaviour is designed into springs and transmissions before the controller runs.

## Key terms
- **Stiffness**: how much restoring force or torque changes when a mechanism is displaced.
- **Compliance**: the ability to yield under load; the opposite tendency to rigidity.
- **Antagonistic actuation**: opposing actuators influence a joint, drawing an analogy with opposing muscles.
- **Degree of freedom**: one independent coordinate needed to describe a mechanism's configuration.

## Getting started
1. **Study the free material:** David is a research platform; the cited pages do not provide a beginner purchase price.
2. **Watch the demonstrations:** distinguish movement commands from the mechanism's response to contact.
3. **Read the annotated diagram:** locate the different actuator concepts and explain which parts store elastic energy.
4. **Begin in a notebook:** sketch a motor, spring and load; relate spring deflection to joint motion before considering powered hardware.

> **Watch out:** Stored spring energy can move a mechanism after power is removed; do not treat an unpowered elastic joint as unloaded.

lessons.summary: do-mpc is a Python toolbox for building model predictive controllers, simulators and state estimators for nonlinear systems.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
do-mpc is a Python toolbox for building model predictive controllers, simulators and state estimators for nonlinear systems.

![do-mpc animation showing the controlled three-disc spring system.](/img/lessons/robots_simulator_tool_2-do-mpc.webp)
*A frame from the official getting-started controller animation. Source: [Publisher](https://www.do-mpc.com/en/latest/getting_started.html), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Predict before acting**: a controller can consider future motion and constraints instead of reacting only to the current error.
- **Software analogy**: model predictive control resembles a rolling scheduler: solve ahead, execute the next decision, then reschedule when new state information arrives.

## What it is made of / how it works
- **Modular blocks**: define a model, configure a controller and connect a simulator or estimator. The same model description supports several parts of the workflow.
- **Explicit problem**: states describe the system, inputs are adjustable commands, and an objective expresses what good behaviour means under the chosen limits.

| Property | Published detail |
|---|---|
| Language | Python 3.x |
| Core dependencies | NumPy, CasADi, Matplotlib |
| Default optimization solver | IPOPT |
| Tutorial plant | Three rotating discs linked by springs |
| Tutorial motor inputs | Two |
| Supported estimation | Moving horizon estimation |

- **Worked example**: the tutorial starts with three oscillating discs. Two motor angles act as inputs; the controller uses them to bring the discs to rest.
- **Read the plots**: compare uncontrolled oscillation with controlled settling, then inspect the chosen inputs rather than judging only the final animation.

> **Key idea:** MPC needs a model and an objective; the toolbox does not infer what your robot should achieve.

## Key terms
- **State**: variables summarizing the system now, such as disc angles and angular velocities.
- **Input**: a command the controller can change, such as a motor's requested angle.
- **MPC**: model predictive control, repeatedly optimizing future commands and applying the next one.
- **MHE**: moving horizon estimation, estimating hidden state from recent measurements and a model.

## Getting started
1. **Create a Python environment:** the toolbox is free and open source; start with its core features before optional extras.
2. **Install from the official guide:** run `pip install do_mpc`, then obtain examples matching your installed release.
3. **Run Getting started: MPC:** identify the model variables and connect the provided controller and simulator.
4. **Change one objective weight:** compare settling and motor inputs while keeping the same initial state, so you can explain the trade-off.

## Used in
- **First MPC with do-mpc** is a direct hands-on continuation.
- **Model predictive control (MPC)** explains the repeated optimization loop; **Nonlinear, robust & adaptive control** broadens the controller-design context.

doosan-robot2 is Doosan Robotics’ ROS 2 software stack for modelling, simulating and controlling its robot arms.

## Why it matters for us
- **An industrial software stack**: inspect how a real robot vendor connects descriptions, control interfaces, simulation and motion planning.
- **Software analogy**: think of a vendor SDK plus adapters: the same ecosystem exposes robot state and commands through standard ROS 2 interfaces.

## What it is made of / how it works
- **Robot description**: model-specific packages describe the arm; RViz2 visualizes it, while simulator integrations let you experiment without a physical robot.
- **Control interface**: controllers connect ROS 2 requests with the robot hardware interface. Virtual mode uses the emulator instead of commanding a real arm.
- **Planning integration**: MoveIt 2 adds motion-planning tools; it is a separate responsibility from merely displaying the robot model.

| Current documentation target | Published detail |

| ROS distribution | Jazzy |
| Documented Ubuntu release | 24.04 |
| Operation modes | Virtual and real |
| Virtual controller | Docker-based emulator |
| Visualization | RViz2 |
| Planning integration | MoveIt 2 |

- **Model selection**: launch parameters choose the robot model and mode; matching the ROS distribution and repository branch matters before building.

## Key terms
- **ROS 2**: middleware providing communication and tooling for robot software components.
- **Emulator**: software standing in for the robot controller in virtual mode.
- **Launch parameter**: a configuration value supplied when starting ROS components, such as model or operation mode.
- **RViz2**: a visualization tool; seeing an arm there is not itself evidence of physical motion.

## Getting started

lessons.name: Drake
lessons.summary: Drake is a C++ and Python toolbox for modelling robot dynamics, simulating systems and designing motion through optimization and control.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
Drake is a C++ and Python toolbox for modelling robot dynamics, simulating systems and designing motion through optimization and control.

![Drake official demonstration frame showing a simulated robotics scene.](/img/lessons/robots_simulator_tool_2-drake.webp)
*A frame from the robotics demonstration embedded on Drake’s homepage. Source: [Publisher](https://drake.mit.edu/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **From equations to behaviour**: Drake links a robot model with tools for simulation, planning and controller design, rather than offering only a visual sandbox.
- **Software analogy**: its systems framework composes small input-output components into a larger program, like connecting functions while preserving information about their mathematical structure.

## What it is made of / how it works
- **Models**: describe state and how it evolves under inputs. A simulator advances that state; a controller chooses inputs from the available information.
- **Structure-aware tools**: Drake exposes properties such as derivatives and system structure so optimization and analysis can use more than black-box simulation results.

| Property | Published detail |
|---|---|
| Primary languages | C++ and Python |
| Python interface | pydrake |
| Supported modelling | Multibody dynamics and connected systems |
| Tutorial continuous example | One state, zero inputs, one output |
| Tutorial discrete period | 1.0 second |
| Software licence | BSD 3-Clause |

- **Worked example**: the official systems tutorial defines a one-state model with `SymbolicVectorSystem`. Here `x` is state, its derivative describes change, and output simply reports state.

```python
from pydrake.symbolic import Variable
from pydrake.systems.primitives import SymbolicVectorSystem
x = Variable("x")
system = SymbolicVectorSystem(
    state=[x], dynamics=[-x + x**3], output=[x])
```

> **Key idea:** Keeping the model's mathematical structure visible enables tools that a rendered animation alone cannot provide.

## Key terms
- **Dynamics**: rules describing how a system's state changes over time under forces or inputs.
- **Multibody model**: a mechanical model containing connected bodies and joints.
- **System**: an input-output component, potentially holding its own evolving state.
- **Optimization**: searching for variables that improve an objective while satisfying constraints.

## Getting started
1. **Start free:** read the installation page's supported platforms and install the matching Python package in an isolated environment.
2. **Open Modeling Dynamical Systems:** run the small symbolic example before loading a complex robot model.
3. **Simulate and plot:** follow the notebook to observe the state evolving; distinguish creating a model from advancing it in time.
4. **Connect components:** complete the block-diagram example, then move to a pendulum model and controller.

## Used in
- **Model a pendulum and a cart in state space** introduces modelling.
- **Balance a cart-pole with LQR** and **Pendulum swing-up with direct collocation** add feedback and trajectory optimization.

lessons.name: Dynamixel (Protocol 2.0)
lessons.summary: Dynamixel Protocol 2.0 is the addressed serial message format used to command compatible ROBOTIS actuators and read their responses.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Dynamixel Protocol 2.0 is the addressed serial message format used to command compatible ROBOTIS actuators and read their responses.

![ROBOTIS diagram of half-duplex communication between a controller and DYNAMIXEL actuators](/img/lessons/robots_simulator_tool_2-dynamixel-protocol-2-0.webp)
*ROBOTIS illustrates the shared half-duplex communication path. Source: [Publisher](https://emanual.robotis.com/docs/en/dxl/protocol2/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **A motor becomes an endpoint**: your program sends an addressed instruction and receives structured feedback, rather than directly generating every motor-control signal.
- **Software analogy**: imagine an API over a shared wire; the device ID selects the server, and the instruction selects the operation.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **Instruction packets** carry a header, destination ID, length, command, parameters and error-detection checksum; status packets report results and errors.
- **Half-duplex communication** means devices take turns sending; the controller must finish transmitting before switching to receive mode.
- **Unique IDs** distinguish actuators on the same bus; duplicate IDs cause collisions, not two reliably synchronized motors.

| Protocol property | Published value |
| --- | --- |
| Serial framing | 8 data bits, 1 stop bit, no parity |
| Device IDs | 0–252 |
| Broadcast ID | 254 |
| Header and reserved byte | FF FF FD 00 |
| CRC checksum | 16 bits |
| Ping instruction | 0x01 |

- **Worked example**: a Ping with no parameters has length 3: one instruction byte plus two checksum bytes; it checks whether the addressed device responds.
- **Read before writing**: register addresses and data widths belong to the specific actuator's control table, not to one universal motor specification.

> **Key idea:** A valid packet format is only half the interface; the destination actuator determines what each register means.

## Key terms

- **Packet**: a structured sequence of transmitted bytes.
- **Control table**: an actuator's addressed settings and measurements.
- **CRC**: a checksum for detecting damaged messages.
- **Broadcast**: an instruction addressed to all connected devices.

## Getting started

1. **Read the free protocol reference** and identify your actuator's supported protocol and electrical interface before choosing an adapter.
2. **Inspect the SDK Ping example**; set the correct port, baud rate and device ID rather than copying its model-specific defaults.
3. **Ping one actuator first** and record its returned model number before attempting position writes.
4. **Decode the response** against the packet layout, including the error field, then explore grouped reads in the official video.

## Used in

- **Smart servos & serial actuator buses** connects the packet view to actuator networks.
- **Joint bus shoot-out: serial vs CAN-FD vs EtherCAT** can compare communication behaviour, not just whether a joint moves.

lessons.summary: DynaSLAM is a visual mapping system that detects moving objects so camera tracking and maps can focus on the static background.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

DynaSLAM is a visual mapping system that detects moving objects so camera tracking and maps can focus on the static background.

![DynaSLAM published comparison showing dynamic scenes and reconstructed static backgrounds](/img/lessons/robots_simulator_tool_2-dynaslam.webp)
*The authors compare scene inputs with dynamic-content removal and background reconstruction. Source: [Publisher](https://bertabescos.github.io/DynaSLAM/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **People are not walls**: a camera sees both stable scenery and moving foregrounds; treating everything as fixed can undermine its motion estimate.
- **Software analogy**: filter unstable records before building an index; DynaSLAM filters dynamic image regions before relying on them for mapping.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **ORB-SLAM2 provides the base**: DynaSLAM extends this camera-tracking and mapping system with dynamic-object detection and background reconstruction.
- **Two detection routes** use observations from multiple viewpoints, deep learning, or both to identify moving content.
- **Background inpainting** fills regions hidden by moving objects using the scene's static map; it is distinct from estimating camera motion.

| Research-system property | Published detail |
| --- | --- |
| Paper | RA-L and IROS 2018 |
| Camera configurations | Monocular, stereo, RGB-D |
| Base system | ORB-SLAM2 |
| Segmentation model | Mask R-CNN |
| Example datasets | TUM and KITTI |
| Repository licence | CC BY-NC 4.0 |

- **Worked example**: in the RGB-D runner, omit both optional paths for geometry-only detection; supply a masks path to use Mask R-CNN segmentation.
- **Add the output path** to save inpainted frames; the README also allows reusing previously computed masks instead of computing them again.

> **Key idea:** A useful long-lived map should describe the room, not the person who happened to walk through it.

## Key terms

- **SLAM**: simultaneous localization and mapping, estimating camera position while building a scene map.
- **RGB-D**: colour images paired with depth measurements.
- **Mask**: a per-image indication of which pixels belong to selected regions.
- **Inpainting**: reconstructing image regions hidden or removed from the input.

## Getting started

1. **Watch the authors' demonstration** and use their free project page's sliders to compare input and reconstructed backgrounds.
2. **Read the repository setup** before installing; it lists Python 2.7 and older vision dependencies, so isolate this historical research environment.
3. **Inspect a TUM RGB-D example** and its image associations, which pair colour and depth frames before processing.
4. **Compare detection settings** on the same sequence; inspect both estimated motion and the remaining static map, not just attractive reconstructed images.

## Used in

- **Break a SLAM replay with moving foregrounds** uses this exact failure mode as an experiment.
- **Robust, dynamic & lifelong state estimation** asks how mapping survives changing scenes; **Visual odometry & visual-inertial SLAM** supplies the camera-motion foundation.

lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Edge Impulse is a platform for collecting sensor data, training machine-learning pipelines and deploying them to run locally on devices.

![Edge Impulse Studio screenshot showing the continuous-motion impulse configuration](/img/lessons/robots_simulator_tool_2-edge-impulse.webp)
*The official motion tutorial configures the processing and learning blocks. Source: [Publisher](https://docs.edgeimpulse.com/docs/tutorials/end-to-end-tutorials/continuous-motion-recognition), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **A small perception project** can start with phone motion data rather than a complete robot, making the data-to-deployment workflow easier to understand.
- **Software analogy**: treat the workflow like a build pipeline; data and processing configuration become a deployable package, not just a trained weights file.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **Collect labelled examples** of sensor readings; labels tell training which gesture each recording represents.
- **Design an impulse**: this pipeline slices recordings into windows, extracts informative features, then uses a learning block to classify them.
- **Deploy the whole pipeline**: exported packages include configuration, signal processing and the learned model; your application still needs to supply sensor samples.

| Motion tutorial setting | Published value |
| --- | --- |
| Sensor | Three-axis accelerometer |
| Example sampling rate | 62.5 Hz |
| Recording duration | 10 seconds |
| Window size | 2000 ms |
| Window increase | 80 ms |
| Gesture labels | idle, snake, wave, updown |

- **Worked example**: one 10-second recording at 62.5 samples per second contains about 625 three-axis samples; the tutorial classifies overlapping two-second windows.
- **Inspect the confusion matrix** to see which gesture labels are mistaken for each other, then collect varied speeds and orientations instead of only repeating easy examples.

> **Key idea:** The deployed result needs the same signal-processing pipeline as training, not merely the neural network.

## Key terms

- **Accelerometer**: a sensor measuring acceleration along its axes.
- **Feature**: a numerical descriptor extracted from raw data, such as frequency information.
- **Inference**: running a trained model on new input.
- **Anomaly detection**: identifying input unlike the examples used to establish normal behaviour.

## Getting started

1. **Start with the public tutorial** and its prebuilt dataset; this avoids buying a development board for the first experiment.
2. **Connect a phone** through the project's Devices page and QR code; allow the browser to access the required sensors.
3. **Train the four gestures** using spectral analysis and classification, then test recordings not used for training.
4. **Switch to classification mode** on the phone to build the WebAssembly package and run locally, including without an internet connection after loading.

## Used in

- **TinyML gesture/keyword control on an MCU** can build on this workflow; MCU means microcontroller, a small computer embedded in a device.
- **Edge AI hardware & on-device inference** connects deployment choices to where predictions actually execute.

## In one sentence

ESP32-S3 is an Espressif microcontroller chip combining programmable processing, wireless connectivity and hardware interfaces for sensors and other electronics.

![Official ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1 photograph showing the module, USB connectors and pin headers](/img/lessons/robots_simulator_tool_2-esp32-s3.webp)
*Official ESP32-S3-DevKitC-1 photograph showing the module, USB connectors and pin headers. Source: [Publisher](https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esp-dev-kits/en/latest/esp32s3/esp32-s3-devkitc-1/user_guide_v1.1.html), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Code meets electronics**: this chip can read sensors and exchange data wirelessly without requiring a full desktop computer on the robot.
- **Software analogy**: firmware is the application you compile and deploy to a tiny dedicated server; its pins connect that application to physical signals.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **Chip, module and board differ**: ESP32-S3 names the chip; the DevKitC-1 board adds a module, USB connections, buttons and accessible pin headers.
- **Interfaces connect peripherals**: I2C, SPI and UART exchange data with external devices; general-purpose pins provide configurable digital connections.
- **Vector instructions** accelerate suitable signal-processing and neural-network computations through libraries such as ESP-DSP and ESP-NN; they do not remove memory constraints.

| Chip or board property | Published detail |
| --- | --- |
| Processor | Two Xtensa LX7 cores |
| Maximum clock | 240 MHz |
| Internal SRAM | 512 KB |
| Wi-Fi | 2.4 GHz, 802.11 b/g/n |
| Bluetooth | Bluetooth 5 LE |
| DevKitC-1 v1.1 RGB LED | GPIO38 |

- **Worked example**: DevKitC-1-N16R8 has 16 MB flash and 8 MB PSRAM; these board-specific capacities are separate from the chip's 512 KB internal SRAM.
- **Read the exact variant** before allocating buffers or choosing pins; some pins are occupied by flash or external RAM on particular modules.

> **Key idea:** Choose software and wiring for the actual development-board variant, not merely the ESP32 family name.

## Key terms

- **Microcontroller**: a processor with memory and hardware peripherals for embedded applications.
- **Firmware**: software compiled and loaded onto the device.
- **GPIO**: a general-purpose input/output pin.
- **PSRAM**: additional RAM available on certain modules.

## Getting started

1. **Identify the board and USB connector**; hardware price is unknown here, while Espressif provides public setup documentation.
2. **Install ESP-IDF** following the ESP32-S3 guide, using its supported toolchain and build tools rather than guessing a desktop compiler target.

4. **Inspect the board pin table** and choose an available interface for a small sensor experiment.

lessons.summary: Eureka uses a coding language model to generate and improve reward functions that train robot policies through reinforcement learning in simulation.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Eureka uses a coding language model to generate and improve reward functions that train robot policies through reinforcement learning in simulation.

![Published Eureka demonstration image of the simulated Shadow Hand](/img/lessons/robots_simulator_tool_2-eureka.webp)
*Published Eureka demonstration image of the simulated Shadow Hand. Source: [Publisher](https://eureka-research.github.io/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Specifying success is hard**: a reward gives numerical feedback during learning; a badly chosen score can encourage behaviour different from the intended task.
- **Software analogy**: treat rewards like scoring functions in an optimization test harness; Eureka proposes code changes, runs experiments and uses their results to revise them.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **Inputs provide context**: environment source code and a natural-language task description tell the coding model what state is available and what behaviour is wanted.
- **Candidate rewards become code**: the system trains policies using proposed functions in GPU-accelerated Isaac Gym simulation, then summarizes the training results.
- **Reward reflection closes the loop**: those summaries guide the language model's next revisions; the model writes rewards rather than directly commanding each joint.

| Published research property | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Paper venue | ICLR 2024 |
| Evaluation tasks | 29 |
| Robot morphologies | 10 |
| Original coding model | GPT-4 |
| Demonstrated hand | Shadow Hand |
| Reference-code licence | MIT |

- **Worked example**: the README's Shadow Hand run requests four candidate rewards per iteration and two iterations, giving eight generated candidates to evaluate across the search.
- **Separate reward and policy**: the reward scores behaviour; the trained policy chooses actions, so a successful code-generation call does not itself produce a skilled robot.

> **Key idea:** Improving the training score is useful only when the resulting behaviour matches the task you actually wanted.

## Key terms

- **Reward function**: code assigning a numerical score to the robot's situation or actions.
- **Policy**: the rule mapping observations to actions.
- **Reinforcement learning**: learning behaviour through interaction and reward feedback.
- **Curriculum**: training through staged tasks, such as pen reorientation before pen spinning.

## Getting started

1. **Watch the project-page demonstrations** and compare generated reward code with the behaviour it trains before considering an installation.
2. **Read the repository requirements**: its reference setup uses Isaac Gym and an OpenAI API; GPU and API costs are not included with public code.
3. **Inspect a saved reward** alongside its task description, identifying what each component encourages and what it leaves unspecified.
4. **Review setup compatibility** before reproducing historical commands; the README's named model versions are not a promise of present API availability.

## Used in

- **Eureka reward-code safety tournament** and **Reward hacking museum** can examine whether improved numerical scores conceal undesirable behaviours.

## In one sentence

Exwayz Engine is a commercial LiDAR software stack for building three-dimensional maps and locating robots within them.

![Official Exwayz mapping visualization of a three-dimensional point cloud](/img/lessons/robots_simulator_tool_2-exwayz-engine.webp)
*Official Exwayz mapping visualization of a three-dimensional point cloud. Source: [Publisher](https://exwayz.fr/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **SLAM becomes an integration product**: instead of writing the whole estimator, a robotics team connects sensor recordings, mapping tools and live localization outputs.
- **Software analogy**: mapping builds a spatial index offline; localization queries that reference online to estimate where the robot is now.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **Mapping consumes recordings**: command-line tools estimate motion from LiDAR data, detect revisited places and combine observations into a dense point-cloud map.
- **Localization consumes live scans**: the embedded component matches observations against the reference map and publishes position, orientation and algorithm status.
- **Separate deployment roles** let mapping run on a workstation while localization runs on the robot; the product page specifies CPU-only localization without requiring a GPU.

| Public SDK property | Published detail |
| --- | --- |
| Mapping delivery | Linux command-line executable |
| Localization integration | ROS package or RTMaps module |
| LiDAR input message | sensor_msgs/PointCloud2 |
| Pose output message | nav_msgs/Odometry |
| Pose dimensions | 6 degrees of freedom |
| Merged map examples | LAS files |

- **Worked example**: the indoor workflow has three stages: `exwayz_slam` writes trajectory and frames, `exwayz_loop_closure` corrects drift, then `exwayz_merge_cloud` writes `map_indoor.las`.
- **Outdoor georeferencing adds a stage** that combines satellite-position observations with loop-closure information; LiDAR-only localization does not mean every map-building workflow ignores other sensors.

> **Key idea:** Building a reference map and estimating a live pose against it are different jobs with different deployment requirements.

## Key terms

- **LiDAR**: a laser-ranging sensor that measures surrounding surfaces.
- **Point cloud**: a collection of measured three-dimensional points.
- **Loop closure**: recognizing a previously visited place to correct accumulated drift.
- **Pose**: position and orientation, here with three coordinates for each.

lessons.summary: FANUC ROBOGUIDE is offline programming and simulation software for designing robot workcells and testing FANUC robot programs before installation.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

FANUC ROBOGUIDE is offline programming and simulation software for designing robot workcells and testing FANUC robot programs before installation.

![Official FANUC image illustrating the ROBOGUIDE robot simulation environment](/img/lessons/robots_simulator_tool_2-fanuc-roboguide.webp)
*Official FANUC image illustrating the ROBOGUIDE robot simulation environment. Source: [Publisher](https://www.fanuc.eu/eu-en/accessory/software/simulation-software-roboguide), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **A workcell is more than an arm**: tools, fixtures, conveyors and surrounding geometry determine whether a programmed industrial task is feasible.
- **Software analogy**: think of a staging environment with a virtual controller; you test program execution and the surrounding system before deploying to production hardware.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **Build a virtual cell** by selecting robot models and controllers, adding tooling and importing CAD geometry representing parts and equipment.
- **Run programs offline** with the virtual controller to inspect motion, evaluate cycle times and adjust layouts without occupying the physical robot.
- **Choose application plug-ins** for specialized work: handling, welding, painting and palletising have different tooling and programming requirements.

| Published software feature | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Visualization | 3D workcell simulation |
| Cell scope | Single or multiple robots |
| Controller | Virtual controller for program and cycle-time evaluation |
| Geometry input | CAD models |
| Included handling tool | HandlingPRO |
| Palletising tool | PalletPRO |

- **Worked example**: model a robot loading a part into a fixture, simulate its program, then move the fixture and compare the resulting path and cycle time.
- **Separate the questions**: reaching the fixture, avoiding surrounding geometry and meeting cycle time are distinct checks; an attractive animation does not answer all three.

> **Key idea:** Offline programming is most useful when the surrounding cell is modelled accurately, not when only the robot arm looks convincing.

## Key terms

- **Workcell**: the robot and the equipment around its task.
- **CAD**: computer-aided design, used here to provide three-dimensional geometry.
- **Cycle time**: the duration of one repeated operation.
- **Offline programming**: preparing robot programs away from the physical robot controller.

## Getting started

1. **Watch a cell-creation tutorial** to recognize the interface and workflow before seeking a software licence.
2. **Review FANUC's product page** for trial access and application-specific plug-ins; commercial pricing is unknown here.
3. **Create a minimal virtual cell** containing one robot, one tool and one part before importing an entire factory layout.
4. **Create and simulate a short program**, then change one cell element and observe whether the motion and cycle time remain suitable.

## Used in

- **FANUC** is the associated organization in the map; ROBOGUIDE exposes its industrial programming and workcell-planning workflow.
- **Application-specific studies** can compare handling with palletising or welding without assuming that all tasks share the same plug-ins and controller options.

> **Watch out:** A successful virtual run does not replace physical workcell safety validation before real robot operation.

lessons.name: FAST tokenizer
lessons.summary: FAST tokenizer compresses chunks of continuous robot actions into discrete tokens that sequence models can learn to predict.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

FAST tokenizer compresses chunks of continuous robot actions into discrete tokens that sequence models can learn to predict.

![Published FAST paper figure explaining action-sequence tokenization and robot learning](/img/lessons/robots_simulator_tool_2-fast-tokenizer.webp)
*Published FAST paper figure explaining action-sequence tokenization and robot learning. Source: [Publisher](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.09747v1), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Actions are not words**: a robot command is usually a vector of numbers; a language-style model needs a representation that converts those numbers into tokens.
- **Software analogy**: FAST acts like a compression codec between a numerical time series and a token-based model, rather than being the robot controller itself.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **Transform the chunk**: the discrete cosine transform expresses each action channel as frequency components, capturing patterns across time rather than treating every sample independently.
- **Quantize and compress**: round those components, flatten them and apply byte-pair encoding to obtain dense discrete action tokens.
- **Decode back to actions**: reconstruction needs both the number of timesteps and the action dimension; compressing actions is separate from choosing good actions.

| Released tokenizer detail | Published value |
| --- | --- |
| Expanded name | Frequency-space Action Sequence Tokenization |
| Universal release | FAST+ |
| FAST+ training data | 1 million real robot action sequences |
| Recommended chunk | 1 second |
| Recommended input range | Normalized to [-1, 1] |
| Model-card example shape | 256 × 50 × 14 |

- **Worked example**: the example shape means 256 chunks, each containing 50 timesteps with 14 action values per timestep; tokens encode each whole chunk.
- **Compare reconstruction** against the original normalized actions before training a policy; rounding means an encode/decode cycle need not preserve every number exactly.

> **Key idea:** FAST changes how actions are represented for learning; it does not supply a trained robot policy by itself.

## Key terms

- **Action chunk**: a short sequence of robot commands.
- **Token**: a discrete symbol represented by an integer identifier.
- **Quantization**: replacing continuous values with a finite set of representable values.
- **Byte-pair encoding**: compression that merges recurring symbol sequences.

## Getting started

1. **Watch the authors' demonstrations** on the research page and distinguish the tokenizer from the complete vision-language-action policy using it.
2. **Read the public model card** and install its listed Python dependencies in an isolated environment; this exercise needs no physical robot.
3. **Inspect the processor source** before loading custom code through `trust_remote_code=True`, then encode the card's dummy action data.
4. **Decode and plot a channel**, checking input normalization and shape metadata before testing recorded robot commands.

## Used in

- **Action chunking & action tokenization** explains the representation problem.
- **FAST action compression oscilloscope** and **Frequency-aware token allocation study** can compare reconstructed signals and token counts across action patterns.

lessons.name: FAST-LIO2
lessons.summary: FAST-LIO2 estimates sensor motion and builds a point-cloud map by combining laser scans with inertial measurements in an iterated filter.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

FAST-LIO2 estimates sensor motion and builds a point-cloud map by combining laser scans with inertial measurements in an iterated filter.

![FAST-LIO repository visualization of an indoor point-cloud mapping result](/img/lessons/robots_simulator_tool_2-fast-lio2.webp)
*FAST-LIO repository visualization of an indoor point-cloud mapping result. Source: [Publisher](https://github.com/hku-mars/FAST_LIO), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Motion needs a reference**: a mobile robot must estimate how it moves before its sensor observations can become a consistent map.
- **Software analogy**: an inertial prediction is a cached estimate; each new laser scan provides evidence that updates the estimate and the spatial index.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **Predict with the IMU**: an inertial measurement unit supplies acceleration and angular-motion observations between laser scans.
- **Register raw points**: FAST-LIO2 aligns LiDAR points directly to the map instead of requiring a separate edge-and-plane feature-extraction stage.
- **Update the filter and map**: an iterated Kalman filter refines the estimated state; the incremental k-d tree supports inserting and removing map points efficiently.

| Reference implementation property | Published detail |
| --- | --- |
| Main inputs | LiDAR points and IMU data |
| Estimation approach | Tightly coupled iterated Kalman filter |
| Map structure | ikd-Tree |
| Supported sensor patterns | Spinning and solid-state LiDAR |
| Example replay | Livox Avia ROS bag |
| Saved point-cloud file | scans.pcd |

- **Worked example**: the documented Avia replay launches `mapping_avia.launch`, then plays a recorded bag; the configuration selects `/livox/lidar` and `/livox/imu` as input topics.
- **Preserve per-point timing**: scans are collected while the sensor moves, so individual point timestamps matter for compensating motion within a scan.
- **Check calibration**: the configured translation and rotation describe the LiDAR relative to the IMU, not arbitrary mounting dimensions you can copy between rigs.

> **Key idea:** Correct timestamps and sensor-to-sensor geometry are part of the estimator's input, not optional cleanup after mapping.

## Key terms

- **LiDAR**: laser-based ranging that measures surrounding surfaces.
- **Odometry**: estimating motion incrementally from sensor observations.
- **Point cloud**: a collection of three-dimensional measured points.
- **Extrinsic calibration**: the fixed position and orientation between sensors.

## Getting started

1. **Watch the authors' FAST-LIO2 video** and inspect the public repository's recorded-data examples before buying sensors.
2. **Prepare a compatible environment** from the repository requirements; its documented launch commands use ROS 1, not interchangeable ROS 2 commands.
3. **Replay a supplied example** with matching topics, timestamps and configuration, keeping the known sensor geometry rather than guessing new values.
4. **Inspect trajectory and map output**, then save the point cloud; evaluate motion accuracy separately from how dense the visualization looks.

## Used in

- **Compare lidar filtering and smoothing on one bag** can contrast this filter-based approach with another estimator on identical recordings.
- **Estimator calibration, timing & observability** and **3D lidar-inertial odometry & mapping** explain prerequisites for interpreting the results.

lessons.name: FAST-LIVO2
lessons.summary: FAST-LIVO2 combines laser scans, inertial measurements and camera images to estimate motion and reconstruct a three-dimensional environment.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

FAST-LIVO2 combines laser scans, inertial measurements and camera images to estimate motion and reconstruct a three-dimensional environment.

![Official FAST-LIVO2 framework diagram showing the multisensor estimation pipeline](/img/lessons/robots_simulator_tool_2-fast-livo2.webp)
*Official FAST-LIVO2 framework diagram showing the multisensor estimation pipeline. Source: [Publisher](https://github.com/hku-mars/FAST-LIVO2), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Different sensors provide different evidence**: cameras observe appearance, lasers measure scene geometry, and inertial sensors describe motion between those observations.
- **Software analogy**: merging three event streams only works if their timestamps and coordinate conventions agree; adding streams does not automatically improve the result.

## What it is made of / how it works

- **Predict and update**: inertial data predicts state, then LiDAR and image measurements update an error-state iterated Kalman filter sequentially.
- **Use direct measurements**: the laser module registers raw points; the visual module minimizes brightness differences between image patches rather than extracting corner descriptors.
- **Share one voxel map**: three-dimensional cells organize geometric points and their associated image patches so both measurement types refer to the same scene.

| Published framework property | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| Sensor streams | LiDAR, IMU, camera |
| Filter update | Sequential LiDAR and visual updates |
| Shared representation | Unified voxel map |
| Visual comparison | Direct photometric error |
| Code release | 23 January 2025 |
| Main code licence | GPLv2 |

- **Worked example**: the handheld rig records `/livox/lidar`, `/livox/imu` and `left_camera/image` together; these are three related streams, not three independent maps.
- **Synchronization happens at acquisition**: the associated hardware repository provides a trigger scheme, microcontroller code and wiring instructions, not just a software launch file.
- **Calibration links frames**: LiDAR-camera extrinsic parameters belong in the configuration; a sharp image cannot compensate for incorrect sensor alignment.

> **Key idea:** Multisensor fusion starts with well-aligned measurements in time and space, before any sophisticated estimation algorithm runs.

## Key terms

- **IMU**: an inertial measurement unit sensing acceleration and angular motion.
- **Voxel**: a small cell in a three-dimensional spatial grid.
- **Photometric error**: a difference between observed image brightness values.
- **Hardware synchronization**: coordinated sensor capture driven by shared timing signals.

## Getting started

1. **Watch the accompanying demonstration** and read the public code requirements; replaying recordings avoids assembling a sensor rig for the first exercise.
2. **Follow the repository's dataset links** and documented environment, noting its ROS 1 build and launch workflow.
3. **Replay the example configuration** with `mapping_avia.launch` and a matching bag, checking all three input streams before interpreting the map.
4. **Inspect the rig documentation** before recording new data; treat trigger timing, calibration and image format as explicit integration tasks.

## Used in

- **Engineer a synchronized lidar-camera-IMU mapper** directly exercises this integration workflow.
- **Estimator calibration, timing & observability** supplies the prerequisites; **3D lidar-inertial odometry & mapping** provides a useful comparison without visual measurements.
